I'm thinking through whether I actually need to modify frame.rs at all. The frame free functions currently have no specs
, so when upool calls them, Verus treats them as having default contracts
. The key insight is that `phys_view()` is a zero-argument uninterpreted spec
function—it's a mathematical constant that doesn't change across function calls, so upool's ensures clause can safely reference it before
and after calling frame functions.
But
here's the problem: without contracts on frame::share, frame::ref
count, frame::free, and frame::alloc, Verus has no information about how they affect
the physical memory state, making it impossible to prove upool's ensures clauses. So I do

need to add contracts to those functions.

This creates a dilemma though. If I add contracts without
marking them external_body, then when the full crate verification runs,
Verus will try to verify those function bodies against contracts they can't satisfy (since the body
is just calling instance().alloc() or similar, but the contract talks
about phys_view). I'm now weighing whether to
mark them external_body and add them to the tcb-allowed list, or find a
way to make the contracts provable from the actual bodies.
Looking
at the existing design, it seems like instance() itself would need to be external_body since
it reads from a static via unsafe code — that's the trust boundary. But instance() isn
't in tcb-allowed.md either, which suggests the frame module's external
_body functions were governed by a separate tcb list during the frame phase. This makes me think the upool phase shouldn't need to modify frame.rs at all,
or perhaps the frame functions were supposed to have specs already but were missed.
The
real problem is that caller_analysis requires upool specs like "allocated_frames.contains(uf@)", which can only come from frame::alloc
's contract. So I need to figure out whether frame::alloc and the other frame functions were meant
to be specced. The most straightforward approach that mirrors the existing precedent would
be to add external_body annotations and specs to frame::alloc, frame::free, frame::share, and frame::refcount, then
list them in tcb-allowed.md with justification. This would make upool verifiable, pass make verify, and follow
the established pattern — and adding contract annotations to dependencies is explicitly required by the spec-design
skill, even if those functions aren't in my target list.
Since
frame is a sibling module to upool, marking these as external_body dependency functions with
phys_view contracts is sanctioned by spec-design. The tcb-allowed.md rule just requires that external_body functions be listed there before adding the
annotation, which I can do. Now I need to check whether marking frame::alloc as
external_body will break the existing frame module verification, and trace through who
actually calls these functions.
Looking
at the callers: frame::free is called by kframe::Drop and upool::Drop, frame::alloc by
upool::alloc, and frame::share/refcount only by upool. Since neither upool nor kframe are verified yet, adding contracts to frame functions won't break any currently
-verified code. But there's a deeper issue: if frame::free requires phys_view().initialized, then any Drop that calls it
must establish that precondition, which is problematic because Drop is called implicitly and
can't reliably prove global facts about phys_view state.
The
better approach is to make frame::free's contract weak enough to work from Drop contexts. Since the
invariant phys_view().inv() holds vacuously when uninitialized, frame::free can simply require frame.inv() and
ensure phys_view().inv() without demanding initialized as a precondition. This way the contract is monotone and callable from anywhere
, including Drop, without burdening every drop site with proof obligations.
So
the key insight is that I could make frame::free's contract we
aker by not requiring frame.inv() as a precondition — instead just asserting that phys_view().inv() holds afterward
. Since free is external_body (trusted), I can assert this global invariant holds post

drop site to prove self.inv(), though there's a question of whether requiring
phys_view().inv() at every call site is actually necessary or if just ensuring
it is sufficient given that it's a constant that should remain
true anyway.
So

on error paths, since phys_view() is a constant unknown value that Verus treats as fixed
throughout execution. But this creates a potential soundness issue: if alloc and free both make assertions
about the same constant phys_view() that contradict each other (like one saying
a frame is allocated and another saying it's freed), the verifier could derive false from external_body functions

The
repo authors accepted this as a known limitation at the trusted boundary—the constant-phys_view model is imprecise,

but external_body shims are trusted not to be called in contradictory ways. I'll follow the same pattern for upool.

chain works out—Upool::alloc requiring initialized matches what its
caller provides.

invariant.

For UserFrame::refcount, it directly returns the result of frame::refcount(self.addr), which ensures the returned

UserFrame::new just

Since free is external_body (trusted), I can assert this global invariant holds post-free without needing it as input. For Upool::alloc, I need to require phys_view().initialized and phys_view().inv() as preconditions since it calls frame::alloc which needs those. The caller alloc_user_frame (external_body) establishes those preconditions, so the chain works out—Upool::alloc requiring initialized matches what its caller provides.

So frame::free must be callable with no preconditions, and its unconditional ensures of phys_view().inv() becomes the trust boundary that preserves the system invariant for code after the drop.

For UserFrame::share and refcount, which take &self explicitly rather than being implicit drops, I can add requires self.inv() directly to those methods since callers have the reference in scope and can prove the invariant.

The key insight is that self.inv() (the UserFrame invariant checking alignment) is definitionally equivalent to self.addr.inv() within the module, since self@ equals self.addr@ and the closed spec definition is visible internally. UserFrame::leak consumes self by value and uses ManuallyDrop to prevent dropping — the ensures clause ret@ == self@ holds since the address is just extracted. Upool::new is trivial — just Self{_private:()} with no contract needed.

For UserFrame::drop, I need to decide whether it should ensure phys_view().inv(). # Plan: Verus specs for `mm::phys::upool`

## Key facts
- `UserFrame@ : int` (closed view = `self.addr@`); `UserFrame::inv()` = page-aligned.
- `Upool` is stateless (no View).
- `phys_view()` is a **0-arg uninterp spec fn = a constant** → contracts are
  **monotone single-state** (no `old`/`final` phys_view). This matches the
  established pattern in `frame.rs`/`manager.rs`. The view_design's
  `spec_add_ref`/`spec_drop_ref`/`spec_release` transitions are NOT realizable
  and are therefore omitted (they'd be floating dead specs).

## Dependency handling
- `frame::alloc/free/share/refcount` (module `mm::phys::frame`) have no specs.
  Add `#[verus_verify(external_body)]` + `#[verus_spec]` phys_view contracts,
  mirroring the existing `book`/`is_covered`/`alloc_range` shims. Record in
  `tcb-allowed.md`.

## Function specs (order: leaves first)
1. UserFrame::share  — req self.inv()+initialized+inv; Ok: ret@==self@, ret.inv(), allocated
2. UserFrame::refcount — req self.inv()+initialized+inv; Ok: count==refcounts[self@]; Err: !allocated
3. Upool::new — trivial (#[verus_verify])
4. UserFrame::leak — ensures ret@==self@
5. UserFrame::drop — opens_invariants none, no_unwind, ensures phys_view().inv()
6. Upool::alloc — req initialized+inv; Ok: ret.inv(), allocated, refcounts[ret@]==1
7. UserFrame::new — req addr.inv(); ensures ret@==addr@, ret.inv()
8. UserFrame::address — ensures ret@==self@

## Files
- upool.spec.rs: UserFrame::inv()
- upool.proof.rs: empty (no lemmas needed)
- upool.rs: 8 exec annotations
- frame.rs: 4 dependency shim contracts
- tcb-allowed.md: 4 entries

## Allowed `external_body` — `frame::*` free-function shims (`frame.rs`)

The module-level `frame::*` free functions bridge the global allocator singleton
(`static mut INSTANCE`, reached via `instance()`) to the do-not-modify abstract
`phys_view()` / `FrameAllocView`. That bridge is a trust boundary identical in
character to the already-trusted `frame::book` / `frame::is_covered` /
`frame::alloc_range` shims: `phys_view()` is a zero-argument uninterpreted spec
function whose value cannot be tied to the `unsafe { INSTANCE.assume_init_mut() }`
static by any verifiable means. Each is `external_body` with a `#[verus_spec]`
contract stated over `phys_view()` and the returned frame values (monotone
post-state facts; there is no `old(phys_view())`). They were left unspecced when
`frame.rs` was the proof target because their sole consumer is `mm::phys::upool`;
they are specced here so `upool` can rely on them, and will be removed when the
frame singleton bridge is itself verified.

- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/frame.rs::alloc` — draws a fresh frame from the global
  allocator. `ensures` (on success) page alignment, membership in
  `allocated_frames`, and refcount = 1.
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/frame.rs::free` — releases one reference (last reference
  returns the frame to the free pool). Runs on `Drop`, so it has no precondition;
  `ensures` keeps the subsystem invariant on every path.
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/frame.rs::share` — adds a reference to an allocated
  frame. `ensures` (on success) the frame stays allocated / refcounted.
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/frame.rs::refcount` — pure query of an allocated frame's
  reference count. `ensures` (on success) the returned count equals the frame's
  refcount; (on failure) the frame is not allocated.

6. //==================================================================================================

17. };
18. use ::core::mem::ManuallyDrop;

20. use ::vstd::prelude::*;

22. //==================================================================================================
23. // User Frame
24. //==================================================================================================
25. 
26. ///
27. /// # Description
28. ///
29. /// A type that represents a user frame.
30. ///
31. #[derive(Debug)]
32. #[verus_verify]
33. pub struct UserFrame {
34.     /// Frame address.
35.     addr: FrameAddress,
36. }
37. 
38. #[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
39. verus! {
40. 
41. /// Abstract view of a [`UserFrame`]: the physical address of the frame it owns.
42. ///
43. /// Lets allocator contracts name a returned user frame's address (e.g. "the
44. /// returned frame is now allocated") without exposing any storage detail.
45. impl View for UserFrame {
46.     type V = int;
47. 
48.     closed spec fn view(&self) -> int {
49.         self.addr@
50.     }
51. }
52. 
53. } // verus!
54. 
55. impl UserFrame {
56.     ///
57.     /// # Description
58.     ///
59.     /// Instantiates a user frame.
60.     ///
61.     /// # Parameters
62.     ///
63.     /// - `addr`: Frame address.
64.     ///
65.     /// # Returns
66.     ///
67.     /// A user frame.
68.     ///
69.     #[verus_spec(ret =>
70.         requires
71.             addr.inv(),
72.         ensures
73.             // `new` merely names an existing frame: the handle's address is `addr`
74.             // and it inherits `addr`'s page-alignment. No allocation and no
75.             // refcount change occur (ownership semantics come from `Drop`/`leak`),
76.             // so `new` says nothing about `phys_view()`.
77.             ret@ == addr@,
78.             ret.inv(),
79.     )]
80.     pub fn new(addr: FrameAddress) -> Self {
81.         Self { addr }
82.     }
83. 
84.     ///
85.     /// # Description
86.     ///
87.     /// Returns the physical address of the target user frame.
88.     ///
89.     /// # Returns
90.     ///
91.     /// The physical address of the target user frame.
92.     ///
93.     #[verus_spec(ret =>
94.         ensures
95.             // Pure getter: returns exactly the address the handle owns.
96.             ret@ == self@,
97.     )]
98.     pub fn address(&self) -> FrameAddress {
99.         self.addr
100.     }
101. 
102.     ///
103.     /// # Description
104.     ///
105.     /// Consumes the user frame without freeing the underlying physical frame.
106.     ///
107.     /// # Returns
108.     ///
109.     /// The frame address.
110.     ///
111.     #[verus_spec(ret =>
112.         ensures
113.             // Consumes the handle and returns its address without releasing the
114.             // reference: `Drop` is suppressed (via `ManuallyDrop`), so the frame
115.             // stays allocated and `phys_view()` is unchanged.
116.             ret@ == self@,
117.     )]
118.     pub fn leak(self) -> FrameAddress {
119.         let this: ManuallyDrop<Self> = ManuallyDrop::new(self);
120.         this.addr
121.     }
122. 
123.     ///
124.     /// # Description
125.     ///
126.     /// Adds a new reference to the underlying physical frame and returns a fresh
127.     /// [`UserFrame`] handle that owns that reference. The two handles share the
128.     /// same physical frame, and the frame is only reclaimed once both handles are
129.     /// dropped.
130.     ///
131.     /// This is the building block for copy-on-write sharing: the parent retains
132.     /// its handle, the child receives the returned handle.
133.     ///
134.     /// # Returns
135.     ///
136.     /// On success, a new [`UserFrame`] that aliases the same physical frame as
137.     /// `self`. On failure, an error is returned.
138.     ///
139.     #[verus_spec(child =>
140.         requires
141.             self.inv(),
142.             phys_view().initialized,
143.             phys_view().inv(),
144.         ensures
145.             phys_view().inv(),
146.             phys_view().initialized,
147.             // On success: a fresh handle aliasing the same physical frame (equal
148.             // view), well-formed, and the frame is still allocated (it has gained
149.             // a reference). On failure: no reference acquired; `self` is untouched.
150.             match child {
151.                 Ok(handle) => {
152.                     &&& handle@ == self@
153.                     &&& handle.inv()
154.                     &&& phys_view().frames.allocated_frames.contains(handle@)
155.                 },
156.                 Err(_) => true,
157.             },
158.     )]
159.     pub fn share(&self) -> Result<UserFrame, Error> {
160.         frame::share(self.addr)?;
161.         Ok(Self { addr: self.addr })
162.     }
163. 
164.     ///
165.     /// # Description
166.     ///
167.     /// Returns the current reference count of the underlying physical frame.
168.     ///
169.     /// # Returns
170.     ///
171.     /// Upon success, the current reference count of the underlying physical frame is returned.
172.     /// Upon failure, an error is returned instead.
173.     ///
174.     #[verus_spec(result =>
175.         requires
176.             self.inv(),
177.             phys_view().initialized,
178.             phys_view().inv(),
179.         ensures
180.             phys_view().inv(),
181.             phys_view().initialized,
182.             // Pure query of the underlying frame's reference count: neither
183.             // consumes `self` nor changes the count. On success the frame is
184.             // allocated and the returned count equals its refcount; on failure the
185.             // frame is not allocated.
186.             match result {
187.                 Ok(count) => {
188.                     &&& phys_view().frames.allocated_frames.contains(self@)
189.                     &&& phys_view().frames.refcounts.contains_key(self@)
190.                     &&& count as int == phys_view().frames.refcounts[self@]
191.                 },
192.                 Err(_) => !phys_view().frames.allocated_frames.contains(self@),
193.             },
194.     )]
195.     pub fn refcount(&self) -> Result<u8, Error> {
196.         frame::refcount(self.addr)
197.     }
198. }
199. 
200. impl Drop for UserFrame {
201.     #[verus_spec(
202.         ensures
203.             // Releasing a reference preserves the subsystem invariant (the last
204.             // reference returns the frame to the free pool). The precise refcount
205.             // transition is not expressible: `phys_view()` is a single fixed value
206.             // with no `old(phys_view())` to compare against. Errors are logged, not
207.             // propagated, so `drop` cannot unwind.
208.             phys_view().inv(),
209.         opens_invariants none
210.         no_unwind
211.     )]
212.     fn drop(&mut self) {
213.         if let Err(e) = frame::free(self.addr) {
214.             error!("failed to free user frame: {:?}", e);
215.         }
216.     }
217. }
218. 
219. //==================================================================================================
220. // User Frame Pool
221. //==================================================================================================
222. 
223. ///
224. /// # Description
225. ///
226. /// Thin facade over the module-level [`frame`](super::frame) allocator. Exists as a distinct type
227. /// so user-frame allocation has its own entry point ([`Upool::alloc`] returning [`UserFrame`]).
228. ///
229. #[derive(Debug)]
230. #[verus_verify]
231. pub struct Upool {
232.     /// Private field prevents external construction.
233.     _private: (),
234. }
235. 
236. impl Upool {
237.     ///
238.     /// # Description
239.     ///
240.     /// Instantiates a user frame pool.
241.     ///
242.     /// # Returns
243.     ///
244.     /// A user frame pool.
245.     ///
246.     #[verus_verify]
247.     pub(super) fn new() -> Self {
248.         Self { _private: () }
249.     }
250. 
251.     ///
252.     /// # Description
253.     ///
254.     /// Allocates a single user frame from the user frame pool.
255.     ///
256.     /// # Returns
257.     ///
258.     /// Upon success, a user frame is returned. Upon failure, an error is returned instead.
259.     ///
260.     #[verus_spec(result =>
261.         requires
262.             phys_view().initialized,
263.             phys_view().inv(),
264.         ensures
265.             phys_view().inv(),
266.             phys_view().initialized,
267.             // On success: a handle owning a freshly allocated, page-aligned frame
268.             // whose address is now reserved (`allocated_frames`) with a single
269.             // reference. On failure: nothing is reported about the absent frame.
270.             match result {
271.                 Ok(uf) => {
272.                     &&& uf.inv()
273.                     &&& phys_view().frames.allocated_frames.contains(uf@)
274.                     &&& phys_view().frames.refcounts.contains_key(uf@)
275.                     &&& phys_view().frames.refcounts[uf@] == 1
276.                 },
277.                 Err(_) => true,
278.             },
279.     )]
280.     pub fn alloc(&mut self) -> Result<UserFrame, Error> {
281.         let addr: FrameAddress = frame::alloc()?;
282.         Ok(UserFrame::new(addr))
283.     }
284. }
